plan.contextChunk: This figure contains two side-by-side panels illustrating 2D translation as a geometric transformation in the xy-plane. In the left panel, an orange square at the origin is displaced to an upper-right position by a translation vector t, shown as a red arrow; the transformed square sits at coordinates (t_x, t_y) relative to the original. In the right panel, two successive translations are depicted: the square first moves by vector t to an intermediate position, then by vector s to a final position, with individual red arrows labeled t and s; a third red arrow labeled t+s connects the original square directly to the final position, demonstrating that the composition of two translations equals their vector sum. This figure establishes the additive composition rule for 2D translations, motivating their representation in homogeneous coordinates where composition reduces to matrix multiplication.

authoredContext:
Consider a translation by a 2D vector, $(t_x, t_y)$ as shown in
-translations. We'll denote the coordinates after the
transformation with a prime. In heterogeneous coordinates, we have
$$\begin{pmatrix}
 x' \\
 y' 
 \end{pmatrix}
 =
 \begin{pmatrix}
 x \\
 y 
 \end{pmatrix}
 +
 \begin{pmatrix}
 t_x \\
 t_y 
 \end{pmatrix}
$$

(left) Translation. (right) Composition of two consecutive translations.

In summary, in homogeneous coordinates a translation becomes a product
with a matrix, and chaining translations can be done by multiplying the
matrices together. The benefits of using the homogeneous coordinates
will become more obvious later.

When chaining rotations and translations only we will have a euclidean
transformation (lengths and angles between lines are preserved). A
similarity transform is the result of chaining a rotation,
translation and scaling (with uniform scaling, $s_x=s_y$). In this case
angles are preserved but not lengths. Chaining all transformations
results in an affine transformation. Each set of transformations
forms a group.

In general, chaining translations, scalings, rotations and shears will
result in a generic matrix with the form: $$\mathbf{p}' = 
 \begin{bmatrix}
 a & b & c \\
 d & e & f \\
 0 & 0 & 1
 \end{bmatrix}
 \mathbf{p}$$ Any transformation with that form (6 degrees of
freedom) is an affine transformation. An affine transformation has the
property that parallel lines will remain parallel after the
transformation; however, lengths and non-zero angles might change.

plan.concept: A 2D translation moves every point by the same vector, and two successive translations compose by adding their vectors, which appears as addition in the translation entries of homogeneous transformation matrices.
elements: 2D x-axis with arrowhead and italic label x
2D y-axis with arrowhead and italic label y
orange original square with black outline positioned at the origin
orange translated square with black outline at displacement t from the original
red arrow from the original square to the translated square labeled t
coordinate readout for translation vector t = (t_x, t_y)
homogeneous translation matrix T(t) = [[1, 0, t_x], [0, 1, t_y], [0, 0, 1]]
homogeneous point equation p' = T(t)p
orange intermediate square with black outline after the first translation t
orange final square with black outline after the second translation s
red arrow from the intermediate square to the final square labeled s
coordinate readout for second translation vector s = (s_x, s_y)
red arrow from the original square directly to the final square labeled t+s
composed homogeneous matrix equation T(s)T(t) = [[1, 0, t_x + s_x], [0, 1, t_y + s_y], [0, 0, 1]]
visual highlight on the translation-column entries of each matrix

interactions.teaches: The learner sees that changing a translation vector changes only the square's displacement and the rightmost column of the homogeneous matrix; in chained mode, dragging either vector shows that the final displacement is their sum.

interactions.label: Translation composition
interactions.teaches: The learner distinguishes one translation, two translations applied in sequence, and the equivalent single translation whose vector is t+s.

demo_steps.title: One translation
demo_steps.narration: Drag the red vector t. The orange square moves rigidly by exactly that displacement, and the homogeneous matrix changes only in the entries t_x and t_y.

demo_steps.title: Apply a second translation
demo_steps.narration: Add a second vector s from the translated square. The first square moves by t, then the intermediate result moves again by s to reach the final square.

demo_steps.title: Collapse the chain
demo_steps.narration: The direct red arrow from the original square to the final square is t+s. The matrix product T(s)T(t) has translation entries t_x+s_x and t_y+s_y, matching the single direct displacement.

plan.keyInsight: Composing translations does not create a new kind of transformation: it simply adds their displacement vectors, and homogeneous matrices encode that addition in the translation column.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Use one interactive xy-plane rather than two static side-by-side panels. Keep the visual style close to the source: thick black axes with arrowheads, large orange squares with black outlines, and red translation arrows with italic labels. The original square should sit near the origin in the lower-left area; translated and final squares should appear up/right by default. In single mode show only the original square, translated square, t arrow, and T(t) matrix. In chained mode show the intermediate square, final square, arrows t and s, and separate T(t), T(s) matrices. In composed mode emphasize the direct t+s arrow and the product matrix, highlighting the rightmost column where vector addition appears.
